title: My Plate of Favourite Foods
strapline: A paper plate filled with the food you love — a first, easy way to say something true about yourself.
intent: Children express their own likes and preferences through food, a subject every child already has opinions about.
Choosing and defending a choice — "I like that, I do not like that" — builds a sense of self.
Talking about family meals opens up culture, home life and difference without singling anyone out.
Tearing, cutting and sticking builds the hand strength and control that later writing depends on.
Naming and sorting foods grows vocabulary and early categorising.
implementation: Give each child a paper plate template and a wide spread of food pictures — fruit, vegetables, meals, treats.
Offer tearing as well as cutting so a child who cannot yet use scissors is not stuck at the first step.
Include foods from the families in the room, not just supermarket staples, so every child finds something of theirs.
Let children choose freely — this is a plate of what THEY like, not a healthy-eating worksheet.
Scribe what they tell you about each choice onto the plate, in their words.
Display the finished plates together and give children time to look at each other's.
Return to them at snack time — "you put grapes on your plate, here are grapes" — so the work stays live.
key_questions: What is your very favourite thing to eat?
Who cooks that for you at home?
Is there anything on your plate that you eat on a special day?
What has your friend chosen — is it the same as yours or different?
What would you put on the plate if we made another one tomorrow?

impact.text: Children make real choices about what goes on their plate and can say why.
Children talk about themselves, their family and their home confidently.
Children notice that other families eat differently, and find that interesting.
Children cut, tear and stick with growing control and a comfortable grip.
Children sort and match foods, noticing what is the same and what is different.
Children pick up and use new food vocabulary from each other and from adults.

enhancements: A real tasting table alongside the collage — try the foods children have chosen.
A class recipe book of the family meals children describe, scribed and illustrated.
A shopping role-play area stocked with the foods that appear most on the plates.
A photo invitation home: "send us a picture of a meal you eat together".
A sorting extension — foods that grow on trees, in the ground, or come from animals.
A repeat plate at the end of the year to see how tastes have changed.

playing_exploring: Children choose freely from a rich spread and follow their own taste.
Handling, tearing and arranging invites open exploration of the materials.
active_learning: Children persist through cutting and sticking to finish something that is theirs.
Pride in the finished plate keeps them returning to add and adjust.
creating_thinking: Children group and justify their choices, thinking about why they like what they like.
Comparing plates prompts real reasoning about same, different and preference.
